Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Perceived depression scores improved significantly more in the TRI 360TM multi-ingredient supplement group than in the placebo group.
Sentence: "All assessed perception scorings on psychological symptoms like fatigue, mental stress, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, emotional trauma, mood changes, self-confidence, willpower, and motivation were very significantly (p ≤ 0.0001) improved in TRI 360TM participants than placebo control group."
Measured as: depression perception scoring
Population: Adults aged 20-45 years with one or more psychological symptoms
Intervention: TRI 360TM proprietary nutraceutical combination capsules twice a day, up to 180 days
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 84
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: No consistent interaction between vitamin D treatment and baseline CRP on depressive symptoms across outcomes.
Sentence: "No consistent interaction between treatment and baseline CRP was observed across outcomes."
Measured as: depressive symptoms (BDI-II, DISYPS, self- and proxy-rated)
Population: Depressed, vitamin D-deficient adolescents (25(OH)D ≤ 30 nmol/l, BDI-II ≥ 14)
Intervention: Vitamin D 2640 IU/day for 28 days plus treatment as usual
Comparator: Placebo plus treatment as usual
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 92
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Responses

### Response A
```json
{
 "rationale": "Study A tests a multi-ingredient nutraceutical with no stated vitamin D content or status, so its exposure is not clearly vitamin D, while Study B is a vitamin D trial.",
 "verdict": "off_question",
 "reason": null,
 "also_differs": [],
 "detail": "exposure: TRI 360TM proprietary multi-ingredient nutraceutical, vitamin D not identified as a component"
}
```

### Response B
```json
{
 "rationale": "Study B tests whether baseline CRP modifies vitamin D’s effect, not whether vitamin D improves depression overall, so its null interaction does not contradict Study A’s benefit.",
 "verdict": "apparent",
 "reason": "outcome_measure",
 "also_differs": [
  "population",
  "intervention"
 ],
 "detail": "Overall improvement in depression perception scores versus treatment-by-baseline-CRP interaction on depressive symptoms."
}
```

### Response C
```json
{
 "rationale": "The conflict is apparent because Study A rated perceived depression as a single item on a general psychological symptom checklist, whereas Study B tested an interaction between vitamin D and baseline CRP on full depression scales rather than the main effect on depressive symptoms.",
 "verdict": "apparent",
 "reason": "outcome_measure",
 "also_differs": [
  "population",
  "intervention",
  "comparator"
 ],
 "detail": "outcome: single-item depression perception score vs treatment-by-CRP interaction on BDI-II/DISYPS"
}
```

content.text: {"evaluation":"Study A tests a proprietary multi-ingredient nutraceutical; the rules say a combination product including vitamin D is a normal pair, but nothing here shows vitamin D is a component, so off_question (Response A) is defensible, though the extraction may have included vitamin D. The responses do not use the required schema fields (they use 'rationale' and null reason), but the content matters. Responses B and C both call the pair apparent via outcome_measure; C correctly notes that A measures a single perception item within a general symptom checklist versus full depression scales (a case the rules list as apparent), while B leans only on the interaction finding, which is weaker. A's off_question reasoning is plausible but if the extraction included it as vitamin D-related, apparent is the better call; C is more precise than B.","ranking":["C","A","B"]}
